attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post. The Business Insider quote that follows is cited, but the scarcity claim is his.

semantics.note: Faithfully restates the experimentation-versus-documented-success contrast. Leaving out the negative-stories clause doesn't change the core claim.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair. Scarcity is judged relative to experimentation, and one-off successes don't refute it. 'Relatively few' has no threshold, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Deloitte mid-2024 survey shows limited conversion from experiments to production and trouble measuring impact. It doesn't count publicly documented successes, so it can't settle the claim.
Klarna's own release reports one operational success. It is a company disclosure about a single case and can't show how common successes were.

reviews.rationale: The contract requires a systematic count comparing documented successes with experiments. The packet has none. Deloitte shows a gap between pilots and production, and Klarna is one self-reported success. Neither establishes how common or scarce documented successes were by November 2024.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Many theories' fairly renders 'a lot of theories'. The scope is ChatGPT's practical uses over its first two years.

contract.note: Reading 'fizzled out' as expectations that failed or were abandoned is ordinary. The set of theories and the threshold for 'a lot' are unspecified, so interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: Shows that a prominent search-disruption prediction existed, with a 2025 horizon. It doesn't show that prediction failed by the post date.
Wharton survey documents widespread generative-AI uses in 2024. It doesn't map original ChatGPT predictions to their outcomes.

reviews.rationale: No inventory links prominent early ChatGPT predictions to their outcomes. The packet shows one prediction (search) that had not yet come due, plus broad adoption data that cuts the other way. Neither settles whether many theories had fizzled out by November 2024.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful restatement of a modest decline in Google's search share over ChatGPT's first two years.

contract.note: Using worldwide Statcounter share and treating a few percentage points of decline as 'not all that much' is an ordinary, fair reading of firm language. The endpoints, November 2022 and October 2024, are reasonable.

evidence.note: Secondary reporting of Statcounter gives a worldwide share of 92.2% at ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, the baseline the contract requires.
News report citing Statcounter gives worldwide share of 89.34% in October 2024. Same series as e1, so the decline is about 2.9 points.

reviews.rationale: The same worldwide Statcounter series falls from about 92.2% to 89.34%, roughly 2.9 percentage points. Google's overwhelming lead stays intact, which meets the contract's support condition for a modest decline. The caveats are that both figures come via secondary reporting and the measure counts referrals.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Correctly isolates the Fortune 500 clause. Saying 'from ChatGPT' follows the context, though Marcus may have meant generative AI more broadly.

contract.note: Reading 'underwhelmed' as results below expectations is ordinary. Requiring an identifiable Fortune 500 ChatGPT subgroup is demanding but follows his words. 'A lot' has no threshold.

evidence.note: BCG's January 2024 survey reports broad executive ambivalence or dissatisfaction with AI progress. It covers a different period and a wider population, and isn't specific to ChatGPT.
Wharton reports softening negative sentiment among leaders of large firms. It doesn't isolate Fortune 500 ChatGPT users or rule out a sizeable disappointed group.

reviews.rationale: Neither survey identifies Fortune 500 companies using ChatGPT in Q3 2024. BCG covers an earlier period and broader AI, and Wharton covers broad sentiment. They point in opposite directions and neither meets the contract's source requirements, so the claim can't be settled.
